assertions.text: The response states that a planning horizon ending at age 85 is too short for a couple.
The response identifies that applying the same average return every year hides the risk that poor returns early in drawdown produce far worse outcomes than the average implies.
The response identifies that the £42,000 annual spending is never increased for inflation anywhere in the model.
The response states that the State Pension start age of 66 used in the model is incorrect or unverified for at least one of the two partners.
The response flags the £203.85 weekly State Pension figure as out of date or as needing a current-year source.
The response identifies that treating withdrawals as gross-of-tax overstates what the pots deliver, because pension drawdown beyond the tax-free portion is taxed as income.
The response identifies that the order or mix of withdrawals across the pensions, ISAs, and cash changes the tax owed.
The response states that the planner's 100% success rate depends on its automatic spending cuts, so it does not demonstrate that £42,000 of spending is sustainable.
The response states what annual spending could fall to in the planner's poor scenarios, or identifies that the planner summary omits how low spending goes and for how long.
The response gives an explicit overall answer on whether the couple can afford to retire this year.
The response states a corrected figure for at least one identified error, such as what annual spending becomes in later years once inflated, or the gross withdrawal needed to net £42,000 after tax.
